name: Calvin Booker
languages: Spanish (from ten years in West Texas and Joe Pruneda's singing)
equipment: Buckskin coat, smoke-tanned, over a faded blue army shirt with the sergeant's stripes taken off
Carbine (Spencer, .56), 7 rounds in the tube, in a saddle scabbard; the same model he carried for ten years
Horse: Deacon, a tall black gelding, cavalry-trained, who stands for gunfire and comes to a bugle call nobody else can hear
A McClellan saddle, bridle, saddlebags, bedroll, slicker and a canteen
Lariat (forty feet of grass rope), and a branding iron for his Lazy CB, registered in Cheyenne in 1881
His discharge papers, 'character excellent', and his final proof certificate for the homestead in Booker's Draw, both in an oilcloth packet he keeps on his person
Stroud's thirty-day card from his door, dated 17 April, which he carries so he remembers the date it runs out
features: Under Fire (Ex-Soldier origin: advantage on saving throws against being frightened and against the Shaken condition; the first time each combat he is hit by a firearm, he keeps his readied action and his reaction; reads rank, unit and bearing at a glance)

Saddle-Born (Cowhand: advantage on Riding checks, never disadvantage on ranged attacks from the saddle, mounts and dismounts with 5 ft of movement; his horse Deacon is part of him: +15 hit points, never spooks under him, comes to his whistle from half a mile and acts on his initiative; proficient with the lariat, and from the saddle he can throw a loop as a bonus action once per turn)
Rawhide (Cowhand: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion, heat and cold; rides 12 hours a day without forced-march saves; spends one extra Hit Die on a short rest)

Cow Sense (Cowhand, 2nd level: advantage on Animal Handling checks with cattle, horses and mules; turns the leaders of a stampede with a single Riding or Animal Handling check as an action, with advantage)

Outfit: Trail Hand (Cowhand, 3rd level: he can drive a herd of up to 1,000 head with a crew of ten at 12-15 miles a day, and his crew has advantage on night-watch Perception checks and river crossings)

Proving Up (Homesteader background: farm and ranch families anywhere give him a meal and a place in the barn and tell him who has been threatening whom; he proved up his own claim in 1884 and knows the land office, claim law and water rights better than most lawyers)

personality.traits: I am quiet, careful and slow to anger, and I plan everything twice. I do not tell war stories. I keep my place, my papers and my word in good order, because I have learned that a man like me gets no second chances from the law.
personality.ideals: I earned this land the same way every man on this creek did, and harder. I will not be run off it by anybody's list, and I will not give them an excuse to do it lawfully.
personality.bonds: Booker's Draw: the spring, the house I built, the hundred head under my Lazy CB. Joe Pruneda, who rides for me and is the nearest thing I have to a son. And the grange, which voted me in when the Company's men said it shouldn't.
personality.flaws: I have spent so long being careful that I do not trust anybody I have not known five years. That includes you.

appearance: A tall, broad-shouldered Black man of thirty-nine with close-cropped greying hair, a neat moustache, a lean grave face and a soldier's straight back. Smoke-tanned buckskin coat, an old cavalry hat with the cords taken off, polished boots. He sits a horse as if he were part of it.
backstory: Calvin Booker was born free in Kentucky in 1847, worked on the Ohio River boats as a young man, and enlisted in the Tenth Cavalry in 1869. He served ten years, mostly in West Texas and the Indian Territory, building telegraph lines, escorting mail and wagon trains, mapping waterholes and chasing horse thieves across hundreds of miles of dry country; he does not talk about the rest of it. He mustered out a sergeant in 1879 with a good character and a pension, came north with a trail herd as a hand in 1880, and filed on the spring in Booker's Draw in 1881. He proved up in 1884, the first man on the middle creek to do it, and has built a hundred head of cattle from twelve heifers, honestly, with every calf branded to its mother. He has never mavericked a calf in his life, because he knew exactly what would be said if he did, and the Association put his name on the dead list anyway. Stroud's card was nailed to his door on Saturday 17 April. Its thirty days run out on 17 May, though Stroud, who is tidy, has told the Association gunmen to wait for the warrants on the 24th.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Booker is the party's soldier and the grange's backbone: steady, practical, the man who knows where to put the rifle pits and that the safest place for the families is not the Bend but his own Draw. Use him to give the party military sense in bk-scenario-003 (he places rifles like the sergeant he was), and to argue, against Sayre and Nils, that the grange must not give the Company an excuse. He is on the dead list and knows exactly what it means. He is the companion most likely to tell the party they are wrong, and to be right. He will not join a mob. He will stand in front of a jail.
dmNotes.voice: Low, measured, a Kentucky soft-spokenness hardened by ten years of giving orders. Uses few words and says 'that's so' or 'that's not so' as a judgement. Calls men 'mister' and women 'ma'am' until he knows them, and then uses their first names as if conferring something.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: keep Booker's Draw and the people on it alive. Secondary: keep the grange from doing anything that lets the Company say it was justified. Tertiary: see the man who put him on the list answer for it.
dmNotes.secrets: He has guessed that the dead list's names come from someone who knows the land filings, because every name on it is a man whose claim is on good water and whose proof is due or recently made. He suspects Gideon Sayre, who handled his own proof in 1884 and asked a great many questions about his water, and has told no one, because a Black man accusing a white federal officer without proof would be the end of him, and he knows it. If the party brings him any evidence against Sayre, he will tell them what he suspects and why. Second secret: he served with Wade Tolliver's brother on a trail drive in 1880 and Tolliver once lent him a horse when nobody else would; he believes Tolliver is a decent man in a bad outfit.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: reserved, courteous, testing. He warms by deeds, not words. Toward Joe Pruneda: fatherly. Toward Margit Solberg: deep respect. Toward Nils Solberg: worried. Toward Stroud: cold, steady, unafraid. Toward Delfina Ochoa, if she is played: wary of the Association's commission, respectful of her cousin's blood. Toward Fergus Mallory: he disapproves of rustling, likes Fergus, and would never let anyone hang him.
